summary: This informational memo defines MIB objects for the Dynamic Authorization Client side of RADIUS, which supports the dynamic authorization extensions defined in RFC 3576. It lets management stations monitor those client functions.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes the network boss needs to tell the doorman to change someone's access in the middle of a visit. This is a dashboard for watching the side that sends such orders.

subtitle: Management objects for RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Client side.

tldr.problem: Network access servers need to effectively manage their Dynamic Authorization Client functions, which send Disconnect and Change-of-Authorization requests to enforce real-time access policy changes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB (Management Information Base) module with scalar objects and a server table that allows SNMP management stations to monitor RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Client activity.
tldr.outcome: This MIB complements existing RADIUS authentication and accounting MIBs, enabling comprehensive management of dynamic authorization on network access servers.

today: RFC 4672 is an Informational RFC that remains current and unchanged. It is part of the RADIUS MIB family and provides essential management capabilities for RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Client implementations on network access servers and policy decision points.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for the RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Client (DAC), which implements the client side of the Dynamic Authorization Extensions defined in RFC 3576.

RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is the industry-standard protocol for authenticating network users and accounting for their resource usage. The Dynamic Authorization Extensions, introduced in RFC 3576, allow network operators to dynamically change user access policies mid-session via two message types: Disconnect-Request (terminate a user session) and Change-of-Authorization (CoA) Request (modify a user's access attributes without disconnection).

The Dynamic Authorization Client component sends these requests to a Dynamic Authorization Server (DAS), typically running on a network access server (NAS). The DAC may reside on a RADIUS server, but can also be located on a separate host such as a Policy Decision Point or Rating Engine. This MIB enables network management stations to monitor DAC functions through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), complementing RFC 4669 and RFC 4671 which define MIBs for RADIUS authentication and accounting servers.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS is how networks check who you are. Dynamic Authorization lets the network change your access in real time. This RFC explains how to watch what's happening on the client side that sends those change requests.

sections.title: Dynamic Authorization Overview
sections.content:
The Dynamic Authorization Extensions operate through a client-server model. The Dynamic Authorization Client (DAC) sends Disconnect-Request or CoA-Request packets to a Dynamic Authorization Server (DAS) that resides on a network access server. The DAS processes these requests and responds with either an acknowledgment or negative acknowledgment.

Disconnect-Request messages cause the DAS to terminate a user session, with the session identifier provided by the DAC. CoA-Request messages instruct the DAS to modify the authorization attributes for an active session, such as bandwidth limits or allowed services.

This MIB module defines two scalar objects that count invalid server addresses for Disconnect and CoA responses, and one Dynamic Authorization Server table. Each row in the server table represents one DAS with which the DAC shares a shared secret. The table tracks request counts, response counts, timeouts, errors and other metrics separately for Disconnect-Requests and CoA-Requests, enabling operators to monitor the DAC's activity with each configured DAS.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends orders to disconnect users or change their permissions. The server table tracks how many orders succeeded, how many failed, and how many timed out with each target server.

sections.title: MIB Objects and Tables
sections.content:
The RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Client MIB defines objects organized in scalar objects and a server table. The scalar objects count globally invalid server addresses across all DAS servers: one counter for invalid Disconnect-Ack and Disconnect-NAK packets, and another for invalid CoA-Ack and CoA-NAK packets.

The Dynamic Authorization Server table contains 32 objects per server entry. For each server, metrics are tracked separately for Disconnect and CoA operations. Metrics include: round-trip time to the server, number of requests sent, retransmissions, successful acknowledgments (Acks), negative acknowledgments (NAKs), malformed responses, bad authenticators, pending requests, timeouts, and dropped packets. Additional objects track Disconnect or CoA requests with the 'Authorize-Only' service type and responses indicating the session was not found.

Each server entry includes the server's address (IPv4 or IPv6), the UDP destination port, and a NAS-Identifier. The round-trip time is measured in hundredths of a second. Counters may experience discontinuities when the DAC module starts or restarts, which the counterDiscontinuity object tracks.
sections.plainLanguage: The table tracks for each server: how many orders were sent, how many came back OK, how many failed, how long replies took, and how many timed out.

sections.title: Management and Monitoring
sections.content:
Network operators use the RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Client MIB to monitor the health and performance of Dynamic Authorization functions. High timeout rates suggest connectivity problems between the DAC and DAS. High counts of malformed responses or bad authenticators indicate possible configuration errors or security issues. The round-trip time object helps assess network latency.

By tracking both Disconnect and CoA requests separately, operators can identify whether specific request types are problematic. The pending requests gauge helps identify when requests are accumulating without responses. The counterDiscontinuity object alerts operators when the DAC module restarts, which resets all counters, so they can distinguish resets from actual changes in metrics.

This MIB complements RFC 4671 (RADIUS Accounting Server MIB), RFC 4669 (RADIUS Authentication Server MIB), and RFC 4673 (RADIUS Dynamic Authorization Server MIB). A network access server typically implements the DAC MIB alongside RADIUS client MIBs for authentication and accounting. A RADIUS server implementing dynamic authorization would typically implement the DAC MIB to report on its outbound requests.
sections.plainLanguage: A network manager can check: Are the requests getting through? Are responses coming back fast? Is anything breaking? This helps troubleshoot problems with real-time access changes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MIB module contains no read-write or read-create objects, so there is no risk of an intruder altering management objects through SNMP SET operations. However, some readable objects are sensitive. radiusDynAuthServerAddress and radiusDynAuthServerAddressType can reveal the IP address of the DAS, useful for mounting attacks on it. radiusDynAuthServerID reveals the NAS-Identifier, useful for impersonating the DAS. radiusDynAuthServerClientPortNumber reveals the destination UDP port.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 lack adequate security mechanisms. Even on a secure network using IPsec, there is no control over who can access and read these objects. The RFC strongly recommends using SNMPv3 with full cryptographic mechanisms for both authentication and privacy (encryption) of management traffic. This protects both the confidentiality of the sensitive information and the integrity of SNMP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The server addresses and port numbers exposed through SNMP could help an attacker target the authorization system. Always use SNMPv3 with encryption to protect this data.
